etymology: Hunk, a large piece or lump ("a hunk of bread"), is early nineteenth-century English, probably from Flemish hunke. The figurative sense — a big, attractive, well-built man — is American slang from the 1940s ("a hunk of man"), common in the 1950s–70s and fixed in Boomer memory by Elvis Presley’s "Burning Love" (1972): "I’m just a hunk, a hunk of burning love." By the 1980s it was the standard word for a male pin-up.
biblical_def: A hunk is a strong, handsome, muscular man — the man women swoon over and teenage girls put on their bedroom walls. The word treats a man as a slab of meat, admired for bulk and shape. The Christian observation: Scripture notices physical strength and beauty in men without making them the measure of a man. Saul was the hunk of Israel: "a choice young man, and a goodly: and there was not among the children of Israel a goodlier person than he: from his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people" (1Sa 9:2). He was also the king who disobeyed, consulted a witch, and fell on his own sword. When Samuel went looking for Saul’s replacement, God warned him about exactly this: "Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature ... for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart" (1Sa 16:7). Proverbs gives strength its due — "The glory of young men is their strength" (Pro 20:29) — and the Psalm puts it in its place: "He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man" (Psa 147:10). Paul’s word to the gym generation is balanced: "bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things" (1Ti 4:8). Little, not nothing. A father can encourage his son to be strong, and teach him that the strength God delights in is the strength to keep his word, protect the weak, and fear the LORD — and he can teach his daughter to look for that kind of hunk.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (1940s; "Burning Love," 1972) for a big, attractive, muscular man — a physical glory Scripture grants young men (Pro 20:29) but refuses as the measure of a man, for the LORD looketh on the heart (1Sa 16:7).
webster_full: HUNK, n. (American slang, 1940s; Boomer era–present) A sexually attractive, muscular, well-built man. "He’s a real hunk." Also hunky (adj.).
Older and still-current sense: a large piece or lump, as of bread or meat (early 19th c.).
Decode for families: the male counterpart of stone fox and baddie — and Saul (1Sa 9:2) is Scripture’s cautionary case.
scriptures: And he had a son, whose name was Saul, a choice young man, and a goodly: and there was not among the children of Israel a goodlier person than he: from his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people.

But the LORD said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart.
The glory of young men is their strength: and the beauty of old men is the gray head.
He delighteth not in the strength of the horse: he taketh not pleasure in the legs of a man.
For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.
corruption_summary: Hunk measures a man by his bulk and beauty; Scripture grants young men the glory of strength but measures a man by his heart, and warns with the example of Saul.
corruption_paragraphs: Every age has idolized the strong, handsome young man, and Scripture shows why it is dangerous. Israel asked for a king like the nations and got Saul — tall, handsome, impressive, and spiritually hollow. Absalom too was praised for his beauty — "from the sole of his foot even to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him" — and his famous hair became the instrument of his death. The Bible keeps showing us the hunk and then showing us his end.

The modern version has added the gym and the camera. Young men now curate their bodies the way young women have long been pressured to, and the measure of a man becomes his physique in a mirror. Paul’s word is wise: exercise profits a little (1Ti 4:8). Train the body; but train the soul more. The man God delights in is not the one with the legs of a horse (Psa 147:10), but "them that fear him, in those that hope in his mercy."
roots_summary: Flemish hunke (?) → English hunk (a lump, early 19th c.) → 1940s American slang (an attractive muscular man) → 1972 "Burning Love."
roots_lines: Probably Flemish hunke — a hunk, a lump of food
Early 19th-c. English: hunk — a large piece cut off
1940s American slang: a hunk of man — a big, attractive man
1972: Elvis Presley, "Burning Love" — "a hunk, a hunk of burning love"
Hebrew bachur tov — "a choice young man, and a goodly" (1Sa 9:2)
usage: "Grandma says Grandpa was a hunk in 1970. Grandpa says he still is. The jury is out."
The LORD looketh on the heart (1Sa 16:7).
Bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things (1Ti 4:8).

etymology: From chick, a young chicken (Middle English chike, shortened from chicken), which Webster in 1828 defined also as "a person of tender years" and "a word of tenderness." As slang for a young woman, chick was current in early-twentieth-century American speech and especially in 1940s–50s jazz and beat talk; it was everywhere in the 1960s and 70s ("a groovy chick", "chick flick" later), and from about 1970 feminists objected to it as belittling.
biblical_def: A chick is a young woman — in the 1960s mouth, casual, sometimes affectionate, often dismissive: "Who’s the chick with Dave?" The word compares a woman to a baby bird: small, cute, and not quite grown. The Christian observation: the word began as tenderness and drifted into condescension, and Scripture shows how to keep the tenderness and drop the condescension. The tender use of the image is God’s own. The Lord Jesus wept over Jerusalem: "how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!" (Mat 23:37). The Psalmist: "He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust" (Psa 91:4). In that picture the chicks are precious and protected. But the slang turned the picture toward the man’s convenience: chicks to be picked up, chased, and traded. Scripture’s word for a woman is far weightier. Adam’s first words about her were a poem: "This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman" (Gen 2:23). Peter tells husbands to give "honour unto the wife ... as being heirs together of the grace of life" (1Pe 3:7). A woman is not a chick to be collected but a fellow heir to be honored. A father can teach his son to speak of women in a way that would make their fathers glad, and to remember that under the wings of Christ there is room for sons and daughters alike.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (from jazz and beat talk) for a young woman — once tender, often dismissive — corrected by Scripture’s weightier word: bone of my bones (Gen 2:23), an heir together of the grace of life (1Pe 3:7).
webster_full: CHICK, n. (American slang, early 20th c.; jazz / beat 1940s–50s; Boomer-era common) A young woman. "A groovy chick." Often regarded as disrespectful from about 1970.
Webster (1828) — CHICKEN, noun 1. The young of fowls, particularly of the domestic hen, or gallinaceous fowls. 2. A person of tender years. 3. A word of tenderness.
Decode for families: Gen Z rarely uses it; when Grandpa does, he probably means no harm. Your sons should choose a better word.
scriptures: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, thou that killest the prophets, and stonest them which are sent unto thee, how often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not!
Psa 91:4
He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.
Gen 2:23
And Adam said, This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.

Likewise, ye husbands, dwell with them according to knowledge, giving honour unto the wife, as unto the weaker vessel, and as being heirs together of the grace of life; that your prayers be not hindered.
The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity.
corruption_summary: Chick turned a word of tenderness into a word of condescension; Scripture keeps the tenderness of the hen gathering her chickens and gives women the weightier name of fellow heirs.
corruption_paragraphs: Slang for women tells you how men think of them, and the 1960s vocabulary is revealing: chick, bird, fox, broad. Each makes a woman something smaller or other than a person — an animal to chase, a pet to keep. The sexual revolution, which promised women freedom, came wrapped in this vocabulary, and the women of that generation learned quickly that "free love" often meant being treated as a chick to be picked up and put down. Their objection to the word was not oversensitive; it was accurate.

Paul tells Timothy how to treat young women: "The elder women as mothers; the younger as sisters, with all purity" (1Ti 5:2). That is the Christian man’s vocabulary: mothers, sisters, wife, daughters — family words, protective words, honoring words. The tender image in "chick" belongs to God’s care for His people (Mat 23:37), and men who bear His image should speak with His tenderness.
roots_summary: Old English cicen (chicken) → Middle English chike → chick (a young bird; a word of tenderness) → early-20th-c. American slang (a young woman) → 1960s ubiquity.

Early 20th c. American slang: chick — a young woman
1940s–60s: jazz, beat, and hippie vocabulary; c. 1970 criticized as belittling
Greek nossia — a brood; the hen’s chickens (Mat 23:37)
usage: "Grandpa still calls women ‘chicks.’ Grandma has been working on him since 1971."
As a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings (Mat 23:37).
Giving honour unto the wife, as being heirs together of the grace of life (1Pe 3:7).

etymology: Old woman and old lady for one’s wife or mother are colloquial English from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries ("my old lady’s cooking"). In 1960s hippie and biker slang old lady was extended to a man’s live-in girlfriend or steady partner, married or not — "his old lady" — and the term was common in the rock lyrics and memoirs of the 1970s. It remains in use, usually affectionate, sometimes dismissive.
biblical_def: In Boomer slang a man’s old lady was his wife or, in the counterculture, his live-in girlfriend: "Me and my old lady are moving to Oregon." It could be fond or offhand, and in the hippie and biker world it often named a relationship with no vows at all. The Christian observation: the phrase blurs exactly the line Scripture draws most clearly. Scripture has a word for the woman a man lives with, and it is wife — a covenant word, sealed before God and witnesses. "Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the LORD" (Pro 18:22). The counterculture’s old lady claimed the intimacy and companionship of a wife while refusing the covenant, and Scripture calls that by its name. But the older, married sense of the phrase is worth honoring, because it describes something beautiful: a wife who has grown old beside her husband. "A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband" (Pro 12:4). "The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her" (Pro 31:11). And husbands are commanded: "love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it" (Eph 5:25). An old man who calls his wife of fifty years his old lady, with a twinkle, has earned the phrase. A young man who calls his girlfriend that has borrowed the word without paying for it. The Christian answer is simple: marry her, and then grow old together.
webster_summary: Colloquial for one’s wife or mother (18th–19th c.), extended in 1960s hippie and biker slang to a live-in girlfriend — a blurring of the covenant line Scripture draws plainly: whoso findeth a wife (Pro 18:22).
webster_full: OLD LADY, n. (colloquial, 18th c.–; Boomer counterculture extension, 1960s) 1. One’s wife. 2. One’s mother. 3. (1960s–70s hippie and biker slang) A man’s girlfriend or live-in partner. "His old lady."

Webster (1828) — LADY, noun 1. A woman of distinction. Originally, the title of lady was given to the daughters of earls and others in high rank, but by custom, the title belongs to any woman of genteel education. 2. A word of complaisance; used of women. 3. Mistress; the female who presides or has authority over a manor or a family.
Decode for families: ask which sense is meant. Sense 1 can be a term of endearment; sense 3 is cohabitation with a nickname.
scriptures: Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the LORD.
Pro 12:4
A virtuous woman is a crown to her husband: but she that maketh ashamed is as rottenness in his bones.
The heart of her husband doth safely trust in her, so that he shall have no need of spoil.
Eph 5:25
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
Tit 2:4
That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children,
corruption_summary: The counterculture’s old lady claimed a wife’s place without a wife’s covenant; Scripture honors the wife who grows old beside her husband and calls cohabitation by its name.
corruption_paragraphs: The 1960s did not abolish marriage so much as imitate it without the vows. Couples lived together, called each other "my old man" and "my old lady," had children, and split up when it stopped working. The language of long marriage was borrowed to dignify arrangements that could end on a Tuesday. The children of those arrangements bore the cost, and the pattern has since become the norm in much of the country. Scripture’s refusal to bless that pattern is not prudery; it is protection, especially for the woman and her children, who are most exposed when there is no covenant.

The married sense of old lady is a different thing entirely, and it is worth reclaiming with a smile. A wife who has walked with her husband through decades of work, children, sickness, and church is a crown (Pro 12:4). Titus 2 asks older women to teach younger women to love their husbands and children — and there is no better teacher than a real old lady in the best sense.
roots_summary: Old English hlæfdige (lady, loaf-kneader) + old → 18th–19th-c. colloquial old lady (wife, mother) → 1960s hippie / biker old lady (girlfriend).
roots_lines: Old English hlæfdige — mistress of a household (literally "loaf-kneader")
18th–19th c. colloquial: old woman / old lady — one’s wife or mother
1960s counterculture and biker slang: old lady — a man’s steady partner, married or not
1970s: common in rock lyrics and memoirs of the era
Hebrew ishshah — woman, wife (Gen 2:23; Pro 18:22)
usage: "Grandpa calls Grandma his old lady. After fifty-two years, she lets him."
Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing (Pro 18:22).
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church (Eph 5:25).

etymology: The old man for one’s father, husband, or boss (and a ship’s captain or a commanding officer) is colloquial English from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The 1960s counterculture extended my old man to a woman’s boyfriend or live-in partner (Joni Mitchell’s "My Old Man," 1971). Entirely separate, and far older, is the Pauline old man of the KJV (Rom 6:6; Eph 4:22; Col 3:9): the unregenerate self, to be put off and crucified with Christ.
biblical_def: To a Boomer, the old man is Dad — "my old man would kill me if he found out" — or a husband, a boss, or, in hippie speech, a boyfriend. The Christian observation: no slang phrase has a richer accidental echo in the King James Bible. In Scripture, "the old man" is the sinful self every Christian carries: "our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin" (Rom 6:6); "put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts; ... And that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness" (Eph 4:22, 24). So a believer has two old men in his life — the father he must honor and the old self he must put to death — and it is worth teaching a child the difference. Of the first, Scripture says: "Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land" (Exo 20:12), "Hearken unto thy father that begat thee" (Pro 23:22), and "the glory of children are their fathers" (Pro 17:6). The slang often spoke of Dad with a mix of fear and contempt, the tone of the generation gap. Scripture asks for honor even when a father is imperfect. A father, for his part, should be the kind of old man whose sons are glad to call him that — because he has spent his life putting off the other one.
webster_summary: Colloquial for one’s father, husband, or boss (18th–19th c.; 1960s also a boyfriend) — with a rich KJV echo: the "old man" of sin crucified with Christ (Rom 6:6), beside the father whom children must honor (Exo 20:12).
webster_full: OLD MAN, n. (colloquial, 18th c.–; Boomer-era usage) 1. One’s father. 2. One’s husband. 3. A boss, captain, or commanding officer. 4. (1960s–70s counterculture) A woman’s boyfriend or partner. "My old man."

Webster (1828) — OLD, adjective 1. Advanced far in years or life; having lived beyond the middle period, or rather towards the end of life, or towards the end of the ordinary term of living; applied to animals or plants; as an old man; an old age; an old camel or horse; an old tree. This adjective is placed after the noun that designates the time lived. Abraham was seventy five years old when he departed from Haran. Genesis 12:4 . 2. Having been long made or used; decayed by time; as an old garment; an old house. 3. Being of long continuance; begun long ago; as an old acquaintance.
The old man (KJV, Rom 6:6; Eph 4:22; Col 3:9) — the unregenerate nature, crucified with Christ and put off by the believer; contrasted with the new man (Eph 4:24).
scriptures: Rom 6:6
Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.
Eph 4:22
That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts;
Eph 4:24
And that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness.
Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
Hearken unto thy father that begat thee, and despise not thy mother when she is old.
Pro 17:6
Children's children are the crown of old men; and the glory of children are their fathers.
corruption_summary: The slang often spoke of fathers with the generation gap’s mix of fear and contempt; Scripture commands honor to the father and death to the other "old man," the sinful self.
corruption_paragraphs: The Boomer old man was often a distant figure — a World War II veteran who worked long hours, said little, and ruled by silence and the belt. Many of his children rebelled against him, and the slang carries that tone: the old man as obstacle. Some of that rebellion answered real failures; Paul warns fathers not to provoke their children to wrath (Eph 6:4). But the fifth commandment did not lapse in 1967. Honor is owed to fathers not because they are perfect but because God put them there, and the promise attached — long days on the land — is still good.

The Pauline old man is the more urgent subject. Every boy grows up with him inside, and every father must fight him daily. The gospel does not reform the old man; it crucifies him (Rom 6:6) and raises a new one (Eph 4:24). A son who watches his father repent, confess, and change is watching the old man die in real time — the best sermon a father ever preaches.
roots_summary: Old English eald + mann → 18th–19th-c. colloquial the old man (father, husband, boss, captain) → 1960s counterculture (boyfriend); KJV old man (Greek palaios anthrōpos).
roots_lines: Old English eald — old, ancient; mann — a person, a man
18th–19th c.: the old man — father, husband, master, ship’s captain
1960s–70s counterculture: my old man — a woman’s partner; Joni Mitchell, "My Old Man" (1971)
Greek palaios anthrōpos — "the old man," the unregenerate self (Rom 6:6; Eph 4:22; Col 3:9)
Greek kainos anthrōpos — "the new man" (Eph 4:24)
usage: "My old man taught me to change a tire and to say I was sorry. Both took a while."
Our old man is crucified with him (Rom 6:6).
Honour thy father and thy mother (Exo 20:12).

etymology: Of uncertain origin; it first appears in New York in 1883 for a fastidious, overdressed young man, a dandy (perhaps from duds, clothes, or from "Yankee Doodle"). Western ranchers used it for an Eastern city slicker, hence the dude ranch (by the 1920s). In mid-twentieth-century African-American and then surfer and hippie speech, dude broadened to any man or guy; Boomers popularized it as a general address in the late 1960s and 70s, and Gen X made it an all-purpose interjection ("Dude!").
biblical_def: Dude began as a sneer at an overdressed city man and became the most versatile word in American English: a man, a friend, a greeting, an exclamation of surprise, praise, or dismay. "Dude, that was awesome." The Christian observation: the word’s journey is a little parable. It started as a mockery of a man defined by his clothes — the dandy. Scripture has a word about that man: "What went ye out for to see? A man clothed in soft raiment? Behold, they which are gorgeously apparelled, and live delicately, are in kings’ courts" (Luk 7:25) — said in praise of John the Baptist, who wore camel’s hair. James rebukes the church that seats the man "in goodly apparel" in the best place and sends the poor man to the floor (Jas 2:2–3). Then dude became a leveling word: every man a dude, no titles, no rank. That has a genuine Christian echo, since in Christ there is no respect of persons. But the leveling went too far, flattening the honor Scripture asks young men to give older ones. Paul tells Timothy: "Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father; and the younger men as brethren" (1Ti 5:1). A teenager may call his friend "dude." He should not call his pastor, his grandfather, or his friend’s father that. The Christian keeps the brotherhood in the word and adds the honor the word forgot.
webster_summary: From an 1883 sneer at a dandy to a 1960s–70s universal word for a man or friend — a leveling term that echoes the brotherhood of believers but must not erase the honor due to elders (1Ti 5:1).
webster_full: DUDE, n. (1883; Boomer and later slang) 1. Originally, a fastidious, overdressed man; a dandy. 2. A city dweller on a Western ranch (dude ranch, 1920s). 3. (1960s–) A man, a guy, a friend. interj. (1970s–) An exclamation of surprise, approval, or dismay: "Dude!"
Decode for families: the most durable Boomer word your children use. Teach them the elders who are not "dude."
scriptures: Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father; and the younger men as brethren;
Jas 2:2
For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment;
Jas 2:3
And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool:
Luk 7:25
But what went ye out for to see? A man clothed in soft raiment? Behold, they which are gorgeously apparelled, and live delicately, are in kings' courts.
Gal 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
corruption_summary: Dude moved from mocking the dandy to leveling all men into equals; Scripture shares its scorn for the man defined by clothes and its brotherhood, but keeps the honor owed to elders.
corruption_paragraphs: The leveling instinct in dude was part of a larger Boomer project: to strip away titles, formality, and deference. "Mr." and "Sir" gave way to first names; elders became peers. Some of that was a healthy reaction to stuffiness. But Scripture never treats honor as stuffiness. Leviticus commands Israel to "rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man"; Paul asks Timothy to treat older men as fathers. A culture without honor for age loses the wisdom age carries.

The word’s first meaning still has a sting worth keeping. The original dude was a man who cared too much about his clothes and too little about anything else. James 2 shows the church falling for him, giving him the best seat. A Christian young man can laugh at the dandy and refuse to be one — and he can call his friends "dude" while calling his elders "sir."
roots_summary: Origin uncertain (perhaps duds, clothes) → 1883 New York dude (a dandy) → dude ranch (1920s) → 1960s–70s AAVE / surfer / hippie dude (any man) → Gen X interjection.
roots_lines: Origin uncertain; perhaps from duds (clothes, Middle English dudde), or from "Yankee Doodle"
1883 New York: dude — an overdressed, affected young man
1920s: dude ranch — a ranch catering to city visitors
1960s–70s: generalized to any man or friend in AAVE, surfer, and hippie speech
1980s Gen X: Dude! as an all-purpose interjection
usage: "Dude, Grandpa said ‘dude’ at dinner." "Son, he was saying it before your father was born."
Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father (1Ti 5:1).
Ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing (Jas 2:3) — the first dude.

etymology: From teeny (tiny; also playing on teen) + bopper, a devotee of bebop jazz and later of any popular music (from bop, 1940s). Teenybopper appears in 1966 for a young teenager, usually a girl of twelve to fifteen, who follows pop music, fashion, and fads with breathless devotion — the screaming fans of the Monkees, Herman’s Hermits, and later the Osmonds and David Cassidy. Older hippies used it with some scorn for the kids who copied their style without understanding it.
biblical_def: A teenybopper is a young teen, usually a girl, wildly devoted to pop stars, fashion, and fads — posters on every wall, every magazine, every song memorized. The word was coined in 1966, when the record industry discovered that twelve-year-olds had allowance money. The Christian observation: the teenybopper is a picture of a good thing aimed at the wrong target — the zeal of youth. Young people are made for devotion. Scripture honors that: "Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity" (1Ti 4:12). The question is where the devotion goes. "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not" (Ecc 12:1). The Preacher does not tell the young to be joyless: "Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth ... but know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment" (Ecc 11:9). And the Psalmist asks the question every parent of a teenybopper should ask: "Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word" (Psa 119:9). The industry that invented the teenybopper has only grown more skilled at capturing the hearts of children. A parent need not rip down every poster. But he should make sure the most exciting Person in his child’s life is not on one.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (1966) for a young teen, usually a girl, devoted to pop stars and fads — youthful zeal Scripture honors (1Ti 4:12) and directs: "Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth" (Ecc 12:1).
webster_full: TEENYBOPPER, n. (Boomer slang, 1966) A young teenager, especially a girl, who enthusiastically follows the latest pop music, fashions, and fads. Also teenybop (adj.), of music aimed at that market.
From teeny (tiny, with a play on teen) + bopper (a fan of bebop or popular music).
Decode for families: the 1966 teenybopper had a radio and a poster; the 2026 version has a phone and a parasocial bond. Same heart, faster delivery.
scriptures: Ecc 12:1
Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth, while the evil days come not, nor the years draw nigh, when thou shalt say, I have no pleasure in them;
Ecc 11:9

Rejoice, O young man, in thy youth; and let thy heart cheer thee in the days of thy youth, and walk in the ways of thine heart, and in the sight of thine eyes: but know thou, that for all these things God will bring thee into judgment.
Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.
BETH. Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word.
Flee also youthful lusts: but follow righteousness, faith, charity, peace, with them that call on the Lord out of a pure heart.
corruption_summary: The teenybopper market harvested the devotion of children for profit; Scripture honors youthful zeal and calls it to remember the Creator in the days of youth.
corruption_paragraphs: The word marks a commercial discovery. Before the 1950s there was no youth market to speak of; by 1966 there was a whole industry aimed at twelve-year-olds — manufactured bands, fan magazines, lunch boxes, and a constant churn of crushes. The teenybopper was its product as much as its customer. The pattern has repeated with every generation since, each time with sharper tools, and its business model depends on attaching a child’s deepest affections to a performer who does not know she exists.

Scripture does not mock the young for their intensity; it redirects it. Paul tells Timothy to be an example in purity and faith, not to grow out of zeal (1Ti 4:12). He also tells him to "flee also youthful lusts" (2Ti 2:22) — and the hunger for a celebrity crush is one of the most youthful of them. The best defense is not a ban but a better devotion: a child who has met Christ in the Word has something to compare the posters to.
roots_lines: Teeny — tiny (19th c.); punning on teen, teenager (1940s)
Bop, bebop — 1940s jazz style; bopper, a fan
1966: teenybopper — a young teen pop fan
Late 1960s–70s: the Monkees, the Osmonds, David Cassidy — teenybopper idols
Hebrew bachurot — the days of youth (Ecc 11:9; Ecc 12:1)
usage: "Grandma admits she was a Monkees teenybopper. She still knows every word to ‘Daydream Believer.’"
Remember now thy Creator in the days of thy youth (Ecc 12:1).
Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example (1Ti 4:12).

etymology: Shortened from road manager or road crew, the people who travel with a touring band to haul, set up, and run its equipment. Roadie appears in the late 1960s, as rock tours grew from a van and an amplifier into convoys of trucks, lights, and sound systems; the 1980 film Roadie and countless tour memoirs made the figure familiar. The word is now used for any behind-the-scenes helper.
biblical_def: A roadie is the crew member who hauls the gear, builds the stage, tunes the guitars, and tears it all down at two in the morning so the band can play the next town. No one buys a ticket to see him, and the show cannot happen without him. The Christian observation: the roadie is one of the most biblical figures in rock and roll. Scripture is full of roadies. When Israel moved through the wilderness, the sons of Kohath carried the tabernacle furnishings: "after that, the sons of Kohath shall come to bear it ... These things are the burden of the sons of Kohath" (Num 4:15). They never stood in the Holy of Holies; they carried what made worship possible. Paul says the church works the same way: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee ... Nay, much more those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary" (1Co 12:21–22). The Lord of glory Himself took the roadie’s place: "For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many" (Mar 10:45). Every congregation runs on roadies — the deacon who fixes the boiler, the women who set up the fellowship meal, the man who runs the sound board and is noticed only when it fails. "Whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men" (Col 3:23). The roadie’s reward is not applause; it is "Well done, thou good and faithful servant" (Mat 25:21).
webster_summary: Late-1960s rock slang (from road manager / road crew) for the touring crew who move and run a band’s gear — the unseen servant Scripture honors, like the sons of Kohath (Num 4:15) and the Son of man who came to minister (Mar 10:45).
webster_full: ROADIE, n. (rock slang, late 1960s–) A member of a touring band’s crew who transports, sets up, and maintains its equipment; hence any behind-the-scenes helper.

Webster (1828) — ROAD, noun [Latin gradior. See Grade .] 1. An open way or public passage; ground appropriated for travel, forming a communication between one city, town or place and another. The word is generally applied to highways, and as a generic term it includes highway, street and lane. The military roads of the Romans were paved with stone, or formed of gravel or pebbles, and some of them remain to this day entire. 2. A place where ships may ride at anchor at some distance from the shore; sometimes called roadstead, that is, a place for riding, meaning at anchor.
Decode for families: in church, roadies are called deacons, volunteers, and mothers.
scriptures: Num 4:15

And when Aaron and his sons have made an end of covering the sanctuary, and all the vessels of the sanctuary, as the camp is to set forward; after that, the sons of Kohath shall come to bear it: but they shall not touch any holy thing, lest they die. These things are the burden of the sons of Kohath in the tabernacle of the congregation.
And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you.
Nay, much more those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary:
For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.
Col 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
His lord said unto him, Well done, thou good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord.
corruption_summary: Rock culture made the star everything and the roadie invisible; Scripture honors the unseen servant and shows the Lord Himself taking the servant’s place.
corruption_paragraphs: The world of the 1970s rock tour was not a holy place, and the roadie’s life often included the excesses of the stars he served. But the role itself exposes a lie at the heart of celebrity culture: that the person on stage is the one who matters. Every concert is the work of dozens of unseen hands. The same lie works its way into churches, where the preacher or the worship leader can seem to be the whole show. Paul’s body imagery (1Co 12) is the cure: the hidden members are "necessary."

The gospel goes further. The greatest Person in the universe did the roadie’s work — washing feet, serving, and carrying the heaviest burden of all to a cross (Mar 10:45). A son who learns to set up chairs and stack them afterward without being thanked is learning to be like Christ.
roots_summary: Old English rád (a riding, a journey) → road → road manager / road crew → late-1960s roadie.
roots_lines: Old English rád — a riding, a journey; a raid (see Road, 1Sa 27:10)
On the road — touring, travelling (19th c. theater)
1960s rock: road manager, road crew
Late 1960s: roadie
Greek diakonos — a servant, minister (Mar 10:45, verb diakoneō)
usage: "Grandpa was a roadie for a gospel quartet in 1972. He says the gear was heavier than the theology."
The Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister (Mar 10:45).
Those members of the body, which seem to be more feeble, are necessary (1Co 12:22).

etymology: Jive (1920s African-American and jazz slang for deceptive or nonsensical talk; see Jive) + turkey (a theatrical flop, 1920s; a fool or inept person, mid-twentieth century). Jive turkey, a phony, a fool, someone full of empty talk, is 1970s African-American slang made famous nationally by blaxploitation films and television sitcoms of the decade.
biblical_def: A jive turkey is a phony and a fool — someone who talks big, means nothing, and fools nobody. "Get outta here, you jive turkey." In the 1970s it was a sharp but comic insult. The Christian observation: the insult targets something Scripture also condemns — empty, deceptive talk — but it also is an insult, and Scripture has things to say about that too. On the first point, the jive turkey is a stock character of Proverbs: "They speak vanity every one with his neighbour: with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak" (Psa 12:2); "He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him" (Pro 26:24). A Christian should hate jive — the hustle, the con, the hollow boast — and should refuse to speak it. On the second point, Our Lord drew a hard line around name-calling: "whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire" (Mat 5:22). That is not a ban on calling folly by its name; the Lord Himself called the Pharisees fools. It is a ban on contempt — on writing a person off as worthless. "Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying" (Eph 4:29). A Christian can laugh at jive turkey as period comedy, and he can be honest about jive when he hears it. But he does not use his tongue to treat a brother made in God’s image as a turkey: "Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be" (Jas 3:10).
webster_summary: 1970s AAVE slang for a phony or a fool full of empty talk — a target Scripture also condemns (Psa 12:2), and an insult Scripture restrains, since contempt for a brother is forbidden (Mat 5:22).
webster_full: JIVE TURKEY, n. (African-American slang, 1970s; Boomer era) A phony, a liar, or a fool; one full of empty or deceptive talk. Often comic in tone.
Jive — deceptive, empty talk (1920s jazz slang; see Jive). Turkey — a flop (1920s); a stupid or inept person (mid-20th c.).
scriptures: Psa 12:2
They speak vanity every one with his neighbour: with flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak.
He that hateth dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him;
Mat 5:22

But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire.
Eph 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
Jas 3:10
Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be.
corruption_summary: The insult rightly mocks empty, deceptive talk but deals in contempt; Scripture condemns the jive and forbids writing off a brother as a fool.
corruption_paragraphs: The 1970s comic insult has a serious ancestor. Jive named the con artist’s patter, and Black communities that had been lied to by landlords, salesmen, and politicians had good reason to prize a word for it. The Proverbs share that instinct: the flatterer, the dissembler, and the double-hearted man are exposed again and again. A Christian who learns to recognize jive is learning discernment.

The danger is the second word. Contempt is easy and pleasurable, and comedy makes it easier. Our Lord’s teaching in Mat 5:22 places contempt beside murder in the heart, because both deny the worth of a person made in God’s image. A father can let his children enjoy the old sitcoms while teaching them that the Christian names a lie as a lie and still treats the liar as a man for whom Christ died.
roots_summary: 1920s jazz jive (deceptive talk) + 1920s theater turkey (a flop) / mid-20th-c. turkey (a fool) → 1970s AAVE jive turkey.
roots_lines: Jive — 1920s African-American and jazz slang: misleading or nonsensical talk (see Jive)
Turkey — the bird (from Turkey merchants, 16th c.); 1920s theater, a flop
Mid-20th c.: turkey — a stupid, inept, or contemptible person
1970s: jive turkey — a phony fool; spread by film and television
Greek mōre — "Thou fool" (Mat 5:22)
usage: "Grandpa called the used-car salesman a jive turkey. He was right about the transmission."
With flattering lips and with a double heart do they speak (Psa 12:2).
Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be (Jas 3:10).

etymology: Soul as the name for Black culture, music, and spirit (soul music, soul food) arose in the late 1950s; soul brother and soul sister, a fellow Black man or woman, followed in the late 1950s and 1960s. During the urban riots of 1967–68, Black shopkeepers painted "Soul Brother" on their windows so rioters would pass them by. James Brown was billed as "Soul Brother Number One." By the 1970s the phrase was extended to any kindred spirit.
biblical_def: A soul brother was, in the 1960s, a fellow Black man — a term of solidarity and pride in a time of struggle — and later anyone who shares one’s deepest sympathies. The Christian observation: the phrase reaches for a real good, the bond of brotherhood, and Scripture shows where its deepest form is found. The solidarity of the civil-rights era was forged under real injustice, and Scripture honors those who stand with the oppressed. But Scripture also locates the root of human brotherhood further back: God "hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth" (Act 17:26). Every man and woman descends from Adam; in that sense all are kin. And it locates the highest brotherhood in Christ, where the walls that divide are torn down: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus" (Gal 3:28). The evidence of new life, John says, is precisely this love: "We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren" (1Jn 3:14). The vision at the end of the Bible is "a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues" standing before the Lamb (Rev 7:9). The church has often failed that vision, and the soul-brother solidarity of the 1960s was in part a reproach to churches that would not seat Black worshipers. A Christian father can teach his son that in the family of God his truest soul brothers may look nothing like him — "how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!" (Psa 133:1).
webster_summary: Late-1950s–60s Black slang for a fellow Black man, a term of solidarity (later any kindred spirit) — a real brotherhood Scripture roots in one blood (Act 17:26) and perfects in Christ, where all are one (Gal 3:28).
webster_full: SOUL BROTHER, n. (African-American slang, late 1950s–60s; Boomer era) A fellow Black man; a term of racial solidarity and pride. Fem. soul sister. Later, any kindred spirit.

Webster (1828) — BROTHER, noun plural brothers or brethren. [Latin frater.] 1. A human male born of the same father and mother. A male by one of the parents only is called a half-brother, or brother of the half blood. 2. Any one closely united; an associate; as a band of brothers. 3. One that resembles another in manners. He that is slothful in his work is brother to him that is a great waster. Proverbs 18:9 . In scripture, the term brother is applied to a kinsman by blood more remote that a son of the same parents; as in the case of Abraham and Lot, Jacob and Laban. Persons of the same profession call each other brother as judges, clergymen, professors of religion, members of societies united in a common cause, monks and the like. Kings give to each other the title of brother address their congregations by the title of brethren.
Decode for families: the phrase belongs to a particular moment in American history; use it with care, and teach the brotherhood Gal 3:28 describes.
scriptures: And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;
Gal 3:28
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren. He that loveth not his brother abideth in death.
Rev 7:9

After this I beheld, and, lo, a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues, stood before the throne, and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, and palms in their hands;
A Song of degrees of David. Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!
corruption_summary: The phrase built real solidarity under real injustice; Scripture honors that bond, roots all men in one blood, and offers a brotherhood in Christ that no line of race can bound.
corruption_paragraphs: The soul brother sign in a shop window in 1967 is one of the sadder images of that decade: a man protecting his livelihood by declaring which side of a racial line he stood on. It is a picture of a society divided, and of a solidarity born of necessity. Christians should not be quick to criticize those who needed such words; many white churches of that era had refused Black believers a seat at the Lord’s Table, and that was a far greater sin than any slogan.

But the gospel cannot rest in brotherhoods defined by race, in either direction. Its brotherhood is defined by the blood of Christ, and it crosses every line the world draws (Gal 3:28; Rev 7:9). The test John gives is love for the brethren (1Jn 3:14), and the brethren are all who belong to Christ. A congregation where men of different colors call each other brother and mean it is a living answer to the window signs of 1967.
roots_summary: Late-1950s soul (Black culture, music, spirit) + brother → soul brother / soul sister (late 1950s–60s); 1967–68 shop-window signs; James Brown, "Soul Brother Number One."
roots_lines: Old English sáwol — soul, life, spirit; bróþor — brother
Late 1950s: soul — Black culture and feeling; soul music, soul food
Late 1950s–60s: soul brother, soul sister — terms of solidarity
1967–68: "Soul Brother" painted on Black-owned shops during riots
Greek adelphos — brother; the brethren in Christ (1Jn 3:14)
usage: "Grandpa’s best friend from the Army is a Black man from Alabama. They call each other brother, and they mean Psalm 133."
God hath made of one blood all nations of men (Act 17:26).
Ye are all one in Christ Jesus (Gal 3:28).

etymology: From young urban professional (or upwardly mobile professional) + -ie, on the pattern of hippie and yippie. The term appears in print in 1980 (credited to Dan Rottenberg in Chicago magazine) and exploded in 1983–84 with The Yuppie Handbook (1984) and Newsweek’s declaration of "The Year of the Yuppie" (December 31, 1984). The yuppies were largely Boomers: the hippies of 1968 in BMWs, Rolex watches, and Wall Street jobs fifteen years later.
biblical_def: A yuppie was a young urban professional of the 1980s: well-educated, well-paid, career-driven, living downtown, defined by brand names — the BMW, the Rolex, the brick-oven pizza, the gym membership. The word was often a sneer, and the striking thing about it is who the yuppies were: many of them were the same Boomers who had chanted against materialism in 1968. The Christian observation: the yuppie is the rich fool of the Lord’s parable in a power suit. "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth" (Luk 12:15). The rich man said, "Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry. But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee" (Luk 12:19–20). The Preacher knew the yuppie’s secret unhappiness: "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver" (Ecc 5:10). And the Lord drew the line that no career can blur: "Ye cannot serve God and mammon" (Mat 6:24). Scripture does not condemn hard work, good pay, or city life. It condemns trusting in them. Paul’s charge fits the professional class exactly: "Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy" (1Ti 6:17). A father in a good career can teach his children that the paycheck is a stewardship, not an identity — and show it by what he gives away.
webster_summary: 1980s slang (young urban professional; "Year of the Yuppie," 1984) for the career-driven, brand-conscious professional — often the hippies of 1968 grown rich — the rich fool of Luk 12:20 in a power suit.
webster_full: YUPPIE, n. (1980; popular 1983–84; Boomer era) A young, college-educated, well-paid urban professional, especially one regarded as materialistic and status-conscious. From y(oung) u(rban) p(rofessional) + -ie.
Decode for families: the yuppie’s children called their parents’ lifestyle "selling out"; their grandchildren call it "hustle culture."
scriptures: And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
And I will say to my soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years; take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry.
But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?
Ecc 5:10
He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.
Mat 6:24
No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon.
Charge them that are rich in this world, that they be not highminded, nor trust in uncertain riches, but in the living God, who giveth us richly all things to enjoy;
corruption_summary: The yuppie made career and possessions an identity — often the hippie’s idealism traded for a portfolio; Scripture calls that the rich fool’s error and commands trust in the living God, not uncertain riches.
corruption_paragraphs: The yuppie is the punchline of the Boomer story. The generation that sang "imagine no possessions" went on to build the most consumer-driven decade in American history. That should not surprise a Christian. The 1960s rebellion against materialism was itself rooted in self, and self is easily bought. When the ideals faded, the self remained, and it wanted a nicer car.

The gospel’s answer to the yuppie is not poverty but stewardship. Work hard, earn well, and give generously; enjoy what God gives "richly ... to enjoy" (1Ti 6:17) without trusting in it. The rich fool’s sin was not his barns but his soul — he spoke to it as if it belonged to him. "This night thy soul shall be required of thee" (Luk 12:20) is the sentence no career can appeal.

Hippie (1960s), yippie (1968) — the -ie pattern

1984: The Yuppie Handbook; Newsweek, "The Year of the Yuppie" (Dec. 31)

A man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth (Luk 12:15).

etymology: From Tom Wolfe’s essay "The ‘Me’ Decade and the Third Great Awakening," New York magazine, August 23, 1976, which described the 1970s turn from 1960s politics to self-exploration: est seminars, encounter groups, jogging, therapy, and every kind of personal-growth movement. Me Decade quickly became Me Generation, a label for the Boomers themselves. Christopher Lasch’s The Culture of Narcissism (1979) gave the critique its scholarly form.
biblical_def: The Me Generation is the label pinned on the Boomers in the 1970s, when the idealism of the 1960s turned inward: find yourself, actualize yourself, love yourself, look out for number one. Tom Wolfe noticed that the movement was religious in shape — a "Third Great Awakening" with the self at the altar. The Christian observation: Wolfe was right about the religion, and Scripture had named it. "This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come. For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud" (2Ti 3:1–2). Lovers of their own selves heads the list; the other sins follow from it. The gospel runs exactly the other way. "If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me" (Luk 9:23). "Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others" (Php 2:3–4). And the motive is Christ Himself: "For even Christ pleased not himself" (Rom 15:3). The Me Generation sought to find the self and lost it; the gospel promises that the one who loses his life for Christ’s sake will find it. Paul’s testimony is the anti-Me creed: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 2:20). Every generation since has been a Me Generation; the cross is the only cure.
webster_summary: Label for the Boomers’ 1970s turn to self-fulfillment (from Tom Wolfe’s "Me Decade," 1976) — the "lovers of their own selves" of 2Ti 3:2, answered by the call to deny self and follow Christ (Luk 9:23).
webster_full: ME GENERATION, n. (1970s; Boomer era) The generation (chiefly Baby Boomers) characterized in the 1970s by a preoccupation with self-fulfillment, self-expression, and personal gratification. From Me Decade (Tom Wolfe, New York, August 23, 1976).

Webster (1828) — GENERATION, noun The act of begetting; procreation, as of animals. 1. Production; formation; as the generation of sounds or of curves or equations. 2. A single succession in natural descent, as the children of the same parents; hence, an age. Thus we say, the third, the fourth, or the tenth generation Genesis 15:16 . 3. The people of the same period, or living at the same time. O faithless and perverse generation Luke 9:41 . 4. Genealogy; a series of children or descendants from the same stock. This is the book of the generations of Adam. Genesis 5:1 .
Decode for families: every later generation has been called the new Me Generation. The diagnosis is 2Ti 3:2; it fits all of us.
scriptures: This know also, that in the last days perilous times shall come.
For men shall be lovers of their own selves, covetous, boasters, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, unthankful, unholy,
Luk 9:23
And he said to them all, If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me.
Php 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
Php 2:4
Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others.
Gal 2:20

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
corruption_summary: The Me Generation enthroned the self as the object of devotion; Scripture lists self-love first among the sins of the last days and calls the disciple to deny himself.
corruption_paragraphs: The 1970s did not invent selfishness, but they gave it a vocabulary of virtue. "Finding yourself," "self-actualization," "self-esteem," and "doing what’s right for me" turned the oldest sin into a program of personal growth. Marriages ended because a spouse needed to grow; children were left because a parent needed space. The therapeutic culture that followed has never looked back. Wolfe’s insight was that this was a religion; Paul’s was that it was idolatry with the self in the idol’s place.

The Christian answer is not self-hatred but self-forgetfulness. Php 2:3–4 does not tell the believer to despise himself but to look also on the things of others. The self is not destroyed in Christ; it is crucified and raised (Gal 2:20). The man who stops asking "What about me?" finds, to his surprise, that God has already answered the question at the cross.
roots_summary: Tom Wolfe, "The ‘Me’ Decade and the Third Great Awakening" (New York, August 23, 1976) → Me Generation; Lasch, The Culture of Narcissism (1979).

August 23, 1976: Tom Wolfe’s "Me Decade" essay
Late 1970s: Me Generation applied to the Boomers
1979: Christopher Lasch, The Culture of Narcissism
Greek philautoi — "lovers of their own selves" (2Ti 3:2)
usage: "Grandpa says the Me Generation was real; he spent 1977 ‘finding himself’ and found Jesus instead."
Men shall be lovers of their own selves (2Ti 3:2).
Let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily (Luk 9:23).

etymology: Generation (Latin generatio) + gap (Old Norse gap, a chasm). The phrase was popularized in the mid-to-late 1960s (recorded by 1967) to name the sharp divide in values, music, dress, politics, and religion between the Baby Boomers and their parents, the generation of the Depression and World War II. It quickly became a standard term for any such divide.
biblical_def: The generation gap was the defining fact of the 1960s home: parents who had survived the Depression and fought the war, and children who rejected their music, their politics, their church, and their rules. Dinner tables became battlefields. The Christian observation: Scripture knows the generation gap, treats it as a sign of judgment, and promises its healing. The book of Judges records the first great one: "there arose another generation after them, which knew not the LORD, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel" (Jdg 2:10). That gap was not about music; it was about God. The fathers had not passed on what they knew. Scripture’s remedy is constant, daily teaching at home: "thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up" (Deu 6:7). "One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts" (Psa 145:4). Fathers are warned not to widen the gap: "provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord" (Eph 6:4). And the last verse of the Old Testament promises that God Himself will close it: "he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers" (Mal 4:6). That promise was fulfilled in the ministry of John the Baptist and is fulfilled again wherever the gospel reconciles a family. A grandfather who once stood on the far side of the gap and now sits at his grandson’s bedside reading the Bible has seen Malachi 4:6 come true.
webster_summary: Mid-1960s phrase for the divide in values between the Boomers and their World War II parents — a breach Scripture traces to a generation that knew not the LORD (Jdg 2:10), and heals by turning the hearts of fathers and children (Mal 4:6).
webster_full: GENERATION GAP, n. (mid-1960s; Boomer era) A difference in values, attitudes, and tastes between one generation and another, especially between young people and their parents, leading to misunderstanding and conflict.

Webster (1828) — GAP, noun [ See Gape and Gab .] 1. An opening in any thing made by breaking or parting; as a gap in a fence or wall. 2. A breach. Manifold miseries ensued by the opening of that gap to all that side of christendom. 3. Any avenue or passage; way of entrance or departure.
Decode for families: every family has one. The cure is not to close it by giving up the faith, but to close it by passing the faith on.

corruption_summary: The 1960s treated the generation gap as inevitable and even admirable; Scripture treats it as the fruit of faith not passed on, and promises that God will turn the hearts of fathers and children to each other.
corruption_paragraphs: The culture of the 1960s made the gap a badge. Youth was wisdom, age was oppression, and "don’t trust anyone over 30" was a creed. Advertisers and record companies profited from widening it, and they still do: every generation is now marketed as a tribe apart from its parents. Scripture does not accept the gap as natural. It is a breach, and like a breach in a city wall it lets the enemy in.

But Scripture is also honest that the gap often begins with the fathers. Judges 2:10 is an indictment of the generation that conquered Canaan and did not teach its children. Many Boomers grew up in churches where faith was assumed and not taught, and they left. The remedy is not nostalgia but Deuteronomy 6: talk about God at the table, in the car, at bedtime. Malachi’s promise (Mal 4:6) is for families who will do the slow work of passing the faith on.
roots_summary: Latin generatio + Old Norse gap (a chasm) → generation gap, mid-1960s (by 1967).
roots_lines: Latin generatio — a begetting, a generation
Old Norse gap — a chasm, an opening (see Gap)
Mid-1960s: generation gap — Boomers vs. their World War II parents
Hebrew dor — a generation, an age (Jdg 2:10; Psa 145:4)
Mal 4:6 — the promise of hearts turned, fathers to children and children to fathers
